#862. Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism

Numerous grassroots initiatives in Germany are facing funding cuts. Affected organizations are sounding the alarm, pointing to growing challenges posed by far-right extremism.

Initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

The "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

Numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.

"In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.

The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.

The  Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.

The promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

During the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need new areas of focus," he said. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.

But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, (CLAIM).

The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.

The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself."

If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.

In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available."

However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are currently not seeing. And that is very unsettling."

Many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.

"The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she said.

For organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.

The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.

This article was originally written in German.

Isak and Wirtz are starting to form a profitable partnership, but Iraola believes the overall team performances are helping them flourish.

“The important part is they help the team to play well, to win games, to get results, and if we play well then we have chances, we are solid, everyone will play their part and will look better. Alex and Flo right now are in a good moment.”

#859. 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract

For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

When does Cameron Diaz not sound like Cameron Diaz? When you're in a German cinema.

For more than 30 years, whenever the Oscar-winning actor has appeared on German screens, she has spoken with the voice of Katrin Fröhlich.

The same goes for all other famous actors. In Germany's €125-million ($138-million) voiceover industry, Hollywood's up-and-comers are "adopted" by a voice actor who provides their German voice — often for decades — ensuring continuity and a certain relationship to the stars for audiences.

But on Netflix, and perhaps elsewhere, many of those voices might be about to change.

Recently, Fröhlich and fellow voice actors Anne Helm (Margot Robbie) and Luise Helm (Scarlett Johansson) published a video on social media, letting their followers know they wouldn't provide their voices anymore.

The reason? They refuse to sign Netflix's contract, seen by DW, which contains a clause that lets the American entertainment giant use their voices for training its AI.

They're not the first voiceover artists to speak out on the topic. But they are the first ones to go viral.

"It was unexpected, completely," Fröhlich said. "For whatever reason, we managed to reach people, perhaps because … we are three well-known women in the voiceover industry."

"Over the years, we've managed to make good names for ourselves. It seems to have touched people that we made this statement together," she said.

The new AI clause has been in Netflix's contracts since January 2026. Voice actors sign one ahead of every production. It was negotiated by BFFS, Germany's union for film and television actors.

Fröhlich, like a significant number of voice actors, is not a member and feels as though the union went over their heads. However, BFFS says the deal gives them protection they wouldn't otherwise have.

Till Völger, an attorney and member of the union's board, says previous contracts and those with other streaming services are silent on AI or contain sweeping AI permissions.

If an AI-generated voice doesn't sound like a particular person, companies are free to use the data they have gathered as they wish. Training can take place in other jurisdictions and may not require the actor's consent at all, he pointed out.

"We have a massive, massive protection gap," Völger told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Against that backdrop, BFFS argues the deal with Netflix is a step forward. It allows the company to train its own systems with recordings, but voice actors must give separate, explicit consent before their recordings are used to create actual AI-generated voices, even if the voice isn't recognizable as theirs.

"We've created a contractual right that the law doesn't provide," said Völger. "Is the situation perfect? No. Is it better than before? Yes."

He would like to see other streaming services agree to the same conditions that Netflix has. In his view, only legislation could create the necessary protections voice actors are seeking.

Netflix says human performance "is and remains important to us," in statement provided to DW.

"In recent years, we have commissioned thousands of hours of German dubbing, and we intend to continue supporting a similar volume of work and the use of human voices," the statement continued.

Matti Klemm, the voice of Jason Momoa and beloved children's cartoon elephant Benjamin Blümchen, sees things differently. Like Fröhlich, he is refusing to sign the new contract.

"In short, it says: as soon as I record something for Netflix, I'm automatically training their AI, for free," he told DW. "My job is to create a German original, a dubbed version with my performance, not to train the computer systems of some tech companies."

He is taking Netflix to court, backed by the Society for Civil Rights (GFF), to find out how his voice has been used for training in previous projects.

According to Davy Wang, who is coordinating the case for Klemm and GFF, the lawsuit will seek to stop Netflix using his recordings for training, disclose how previous data was used and establish whether Klemm is entitled to any damages.

The suit will be filed at the end of the year or in early 2027. Supporters donated more than €50,000 to the legal fund in the first week following its announcement.

For Klemm, what is at stake goes beyond training. "It's not about our voice, it's about our soul, our performance, the way we are," he said. "How far have we come when AI training matters more than my actual work?"

Netflix said it cannot comment on a case that has not yet been filed.

For a multimillion-euro industry, the outcome of the case could reach well beyond Netflix and other companies and creative branches are watching. But no matter what the outcome of the lawsuit or contract agreements, voice actors' fears for their future run deep.

Those who don't sign contracts can't work, and streaming companies can make up a significant part of their income.

"Many say: I've held out for 10 months, but I can't anymore. I have to sign this contract, I have to pay my rent, I have to feed my children," explained Fröhlich.

Beyond that, many fear the future of their industry and the connections they have formed with stars and audiences.

"For a many people I'm connected with Cameron Diaz and I evoke something within them," said Fröhlich.

But if Diaz is involved in more Netflix projects, "then I've basically lost her," she concluded. "I'll never be her voice again."

Willian has revealed how Chelsea tried to sign him months before he scored twice against them in the Champions League – and recalled the eyebrow-raising gift he received from a Blues supporter after the game.

The Brazilian winger joined Shakhtar Donetsk from Corinthians in 2007, aged just 19, but admits that he initially had reservations about moving to Ukraine.

Five years later, Chelsea were attempting to bring him to Stamford Bridge. Their January 2012 bid was rejected - but Willian went on to compel them to try again by scoring twice against the Blues in a dramatic 3-2 Champions League defeat that November.

Willian told FourFourTwo: "It wasn't easy. At that time, going straight to Ukraine was not my main goal. I think that every player, especially at that time, who dreamed of going to Europe, wanted to go to Italy or Spain."

"When this offer from Shakhtar came, my family and I talked about it and thought long and hard about whether to accept it. At first, we refused.

"But they kept insisting that I should at least go there to visit the club, visit the city, and learn more about their project. I ended up agreeing."

"I spent a few days there, and I liked what I saw, including the club's structure. There were already other Brazilians playing there too. That certainly made it easier for me to accept the offer.

"I remember that months before that game, Chelsea had already made an offer for me.

"he game was in November and their offer came in January 2012 - but Shakhtar didn't want to let me go."

"So, in the end, I stayed at Shakhtar and kept trying to leave. Then, in the group stage, I ended up scoring two goals at Stamford Bridge, so it was special.

"There's something funny about that day: after the match, a fan gave me a Chelsea shirt with my name on it and a question mark in place of the number. As if to say, 'what number will he wear when he plays here?'

"I thought it was funny and even took a photo holding that shirt!"

That supporter would eventually get their wish, in a roundabout way: Willian left Shakhtar for Anzhi Makhachkala in January 2013 before finally completing his move to Chelsea that August.

#857. German police respond to multiple school bomb threats

Police in Germany are responding to bomb threats against a series of schools, but say that at present they don't believe them to be credible. Danish authorities are reporting a similar series of apparent hoaxes.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Police in Erfurt in Thuringia were among the first to issue a statement on the threats, saying they were responding to threats at "multiple schools" after morning warnings, including in Jena, Erfurt, Mühlhausen, Zella-Mehlis, Nordhausen, Gotha, Rudolstadt and Greiz.

"The same word-for-word threats were received this morning at the various eductional institutes," police wrote in a press release. "Based on preliminary findings other federal states are also affected by the threatening messages."

Police said they had no information yet on the potential author or sender of the emails. They were investigating breach of the peace-based crimes via the threat of criminal activity.

"At present the police is not working on the assumption of the bomb threats being serious and recommends that schools do not implement evacuation measures and continue their normal operations," they said.

Police in Freiburg in the southwest and authorities to the north in Hanover also said they were responding to emailed bomb threats directed against schools.

Similar reports are emerging to the north of Germany in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

This follows other recent cases of coordinated bomb threats against multiple schools that turned out to be hoaxes in Italy earlier in the month.

It also comes amid various apparent bids to create disruption within Europe in recent weeks, such as multiple bomb threats targeting commercial airlines, or hacking into supermarket refrigeration systems to spoil produce en masse.

Joshua Kimmich has criticised Bayern Munich over their handling of teammate Jamal Musiala, describing the club’s public conduct towards the midfielder — who suffers from a neurological condition that causes seizures — as "not Bayern-like".

The comments follow public criticism from senior figures at Bayern regarding Musiala’s performances and contract. The player experienced two seizures on the pitch during pre-season fixtures, prompting opposition from the international players' union, FIFPRO.

A key squad member has now spoken out, warning that the club risks damaging its traditional family values.

"What I don't understand is the way this is being communicated in public," Kimmich told reporters after Bayern's 2-1 Champions League loss at Lille on Wednesday. "It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it's not bigger than a person. That's an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like either."

Kimmich also questioned whether Musiala's ongoing struggles were more closely linked to physical injuries over the past two years, including a badly fractured leg at last year's Club World Cup, rather than his medical condition.

"It's not the case that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself," Kimmich added.

Bayern met with Musiala's representatives on Tuesday to clarify the timeline of events, rejecting speculation that the midfielder concealed his health condition prior to signing his recent contract extension.

Both the club and Musiala's representatives accept that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after extending his contract.

"This took place in consultation with FC Bayern and its medical unit immediately after the neurological symptoms first appeared," Bayern said.

Musiala went public with his diagnosis in August after collapsing on the pitch during two pre-season matches, alarming fans and fellow professionals.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany stated at the time that the episodes were triggered by a change in Musiala's medication. He was rested for the start of the campaign and has since missed games due to a muscle injury.

Musiala came off the bench in the 76th minute of Wednesday's defeat at Lille, capping a difficult week for Bayern. Ballon D'Or winner Harry Kane injured his ankle on Friday and faces months on the sidelines, while Bayern have lost the lead in the Bundesliga and fallen to 15th in the Champions League standings.

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#854. Revealed: Newcastle United NEED to sign this Bruno Guimaraes replacement in January

If Newcastle don't sign a Bruno Guimaraes replacement in January they could find themselves dragged into a relegation dogfight

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Watch Newcastle in their current, post-Bruno Guimaraes iteration and the same problem jumps off the screen. The energy is still there, and St James’ Park can still generate an intimidating atmosphere, but unless the team go direct, things slow to a crawl when the ball reaches midfield.

Losing Guimaraes was always going to leave a dent in the armoury, but the extent to which Newcastle have lost their forward punch is worrying from a black-and-white perspective. And the underlying numbers confirm what supporters were worried about.

According to Gradient Sports data, Newcastle have completed the fifth-lowest number of line-breaking passes in the Premier League this season.

Guimaraes lived for disguising passes through narrow gaps, taking two or three opponents out of the game with a single touch.

Without him, Newcastle’s midfield is a creativity bottleneck. They currently post the lowest completion rate for 'midfield line-breaking passes' across the entire division. Instead of playing forward, the ball gets stuck under players' feet, the tempo dies, and opposition defences are given plenty of time to shuffle across and set their shape.

Not a single Newcastle player sits inside the top 38 line-breaking passers in the Premier League this campaign, as per Gradient data.

Nico Gonzalez is the closest they have, coming in at 39th. He's tidy enough on the ball and offers some progression, but the data shows he is only a partial answer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Gonzalez has attempted just four passes designed to break multiple lines all season, finding his man with only one of them. His numbers against the opposition's back four are similarly modest, having completed just one defensive line-breaking pass from three attempts. He keeps things ticking, but he isn't slicing teams open.

That hesitation in the middle is costing Newcastle badly further up the pitch. In Will Osula and Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Matthias Jaissle has two forwards who are quick off the mark and desperate to stretch games by spinning in behind.

Both players thrive on early, vertical service into space but at the moment, they are making the runs only to watch the ball get recycled sideways back towards the centre-halves. Until someone behind them starts making those aggressive passes, Newcastle are leaving weapons unused.

Nico Gonzalez - Newcastle - 2026/27 Premier League

Sporting director Ross Wilson doesn't need to break the bank to sort it out this winter, either. In France, Lorient’s Arthur Avom has quietly been putting up the exact numbers Newcastle are crying out for.

The 21-year-old Cameroon international is decisive and remarkably accurate. Compare his output directly with Newcastle's current midfielders and the difference is night and day.

Avom has completed three out of three multiple line-breaking passes this season, alongside seven from 10 when attempting to thread balls through the opposition’s defensive line. Just as eye-catching is his overall efficiency because Avom has completed 90 per cent of his line-breaking passes so far this campaign - the same ratio managed by Barcelona's former Ballon d'Or winner, Rodri.

Granted, Avom is playing in Ligue 1, not the Premier League or LaLiga, but matching the gold standard of European holding midfielders for progression in any division is no small feat.

Avom won't cost a fortune as his contract at Lorient expires at the end of the season, putting the French club in a weak negotiating position ahead of the January window.

Even if Lorient hold an undisclosed option to extend his deal by a further year, a winter fee would be comfortably within reach. Guimaraes can never be replaced like-for-like, of course, but if Newcastle want their attack firing again, bringing in Avom - or a player of his ilk - is a no-brainer.

#853. WSL makes agreement with clubs to avoid gambling sponsors

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Clubs have agreed to prioritise sponsorship deals with companies in other industries

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

WSL Football, the organisation responsible for operating the top two tiers of women’s football in the UK, has reached an agreement in principle for its clubs not to make sponsorship deals with betting companies.

Instead, the organisation has agreed to pursue sponsorship deals with brands from different industries, reports The Athletic. The outlet states that six additional sponsorship opportunities were made available ahead of the 2024/25 season, and these were filled by Apple, Airbnb, British Gas, Mercedes, Tesco and WTW.

While the agreement applies to WSL Football’s own commercial partnerships, it does not stop individual WSL or WSL2 clubs from signing sponsorship deals with gambling companies.

Rather, it sets a different direction for WSL Football’s league-level partnerships, giving the leagues the chance to shape their own commercial future. The organisation wants to continue aiding the growth of the women’s domestic game, while combating issues such as player welfare, gambling-related online abuse and fluctuating attendances.

The changes also come at a time when English football is starting to take a wider look at gambling and related sponsorships. At the start of this season, the Premier League’s voluntary ban on betting sponsors appearing on the front of match-day shirts came into effect, while the Premier League, EFL, FA and WSL also introduced a Code of Conduct for gambling-related sponsorship agreements in 2024.

Nevertheless, betting companies still feature prominently among sponsors at clubs throughout the top divisions in the men’s game, with Betway signing a deal with Manchester United and clubs such as Leeds and Nottingham Forest also agreeing new deals over the summer.

Manchester United are in the market for three midseason signings

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United have finalised their transfer strategy heading into the winter window.

The Red Devils are languishing in 19th place in the Premier League with just one win all season, in what's becoming their biggest crisis in the modern era.

With new manager Mauricio Pochettino at the wheel, however, plans are already in motion to improve the squad – with new arrivals coming to Old Trafford in January.

Manchester United were battered at the hands of Liverpool at the weekend in Pochettino's bow, which highlighted the problems across the team.

Leny Yoro was sent off early in the fixture, with Matthijs De Ligt criticised on his first Premier League start of the season, as Pochettino's men shipped four at Anfield.

Now, TEAMtalk have reported that United are prioritising a central defender, a left-back and a striker in January.

Calvin Bassey is high on the wish list – with the Fulham man left-footed – with the likes of Jarrad Branthwaite and Nathan Collins also on the radar.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Benjamin Sesko is out until the new year with injury, with Matheus Cunha starting up front at Liverpool, while Marcus Rashford was an option to sell in the summer but remained at the request of then-manager Michael Carrick.

Ivan Toney and Folarin Balogun are options up front.

Luke Shaw will likely continue as the first-choice left-back with Pochettino having worked with the England man previously at Southampton – though with Shaw now into his 30s and with an unreliable injury record, his days at United could now be numbered.

It is believed, however, that United will not have a lot of money to spend this winter and may have to be clever with players they look to bring in.

Manchester United face Sporting tomorrow night, as Champions League action resumes this week.

#849. Regulator could force Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi ownership out of English football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

David Kogan, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator, says the body has ‘the stomach’ to take strong action against City

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Independent Football Regulator could force Manchester City’s Abu Dhabi ownership out of English football if the guilty verdicts over breaches of Premier League financial rules are upheld.

City were found guilty of nearly every charge brought against them by the league when the commission’s verdict was published in September. A three-person adjudication panel found that the club had systematically inflated revenues and disguised losses by a combined £900m through “sham” deals between 2009 and 2018, aiding their rapid ascent to the summit of the game.

The club have always strongly denied wrongdoing and have appealed against the commission’s verdict. If City’s appeal fails, a sanction hearing will follow and is expected to recommend seismic sporting and financial punishments.

Separately, the regulator (IFR), which was established last year following the fallout from the European Super League scandal, has legal powers to investigate and sanction both the club and any individuals involved in breaching rules.

The IFR grants operating licenses to football clubs and has the power to withdraw them. It also carries powers to order officials who it deems unsuitable to “take all reasonable steps to cease to be an owner of the club” within a given time frame.

The regulator faces a major test of its ability to referee the English game, given both the enormity of the City case and Abu Dhabi’s political and economic relationship with the UK.

Some senior figures within English football were concerned by comments from prime minister Andy Burnham appearing to downplay the significance of the verdict when it first emerged, although Downing Street later clarified that Burnham’s view is that no-one is “above the rules”.

But David Kogan, the IFR chair, has told parliament’s Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee that the regulator is prepared to take strong action against City, if necessary.

“Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue,” Kogan said. “We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size.

“We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that’s been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

“But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so.”

City are owned by City Football Group, a parent company controlled by Emirati royal Sheikh Mansour via his Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) investment vehicle. The commission found that ADUG money was used to artificially inflate City’s revenues, something the club continues to dispute.

Kogan added: “Would I, with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff, that’s been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular issue in our laps this early? Well, probably not. But the truth is, if we don’t act – assuming those circumstances are triggered – if we don’t act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?

“So I think we have to absolutely, clearly be seen to be doing the job that you as legislators have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means.”

City’s appeal against the commission’s verdict has no set timetable but is expected to be concluded early in the new year, with the sanctions hearing then set to follow if any or all of the verdicts are upheld.

City’s most recent statement, on 2 October, read: “Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter.

“The Club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe. The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

“We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.”

#848. COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy

COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good."

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

#847. From sketch to publication-ready flowchart: how AI tools can bridge the gap

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ensar Aydemir is an endocrinologist at Sultan 1. Murat State Hospital in Edirne, Türkiye. X: @dreaydemir

Artificial-intelligence tools can speed up the process of generating publication-ready flowcharts. Credit: -MG-/Getty

When making a scientific diagram, whether I am outlining a clinical study, planning a flowchart or mapping a signalling pathway, I often start in the same way: with a pen and a piece of paper.

Sketching by hand is fast. I can draw a box, cross something out and reorganize a whole idea without thinking about fonts, alignment or software menus. At this stage, my aim is not to make the figure beautiful, it is to work out the logic.

Turning that rough sketch into a clean figure for a manuscript can be surprisingly tedious, however. Text boxes need to line up; arrows need to connect properly; and fonts, spacing and colours must be consistent. A diagram that took five minutes to draw might take an hour or longer to recreate digitally.

Multimodal artificial-intelligence tools can shorten this process. Rather than asking an AI model to create the final scientific image, I use it as a translator. The model reads my sketch, interprets its structure and converts it into editable diagram code that I can open in a vector-based editor, such as Draw.io — a free application for making diagrams.

This distinction matters. I do not want AI to invent a figure for me; I want it to help me to digitize a figure that I have already designed.

One tempting approach is to provide a description to an image-generation model and ask for a polished scientific figure.

For research diagrams, this can create more problems than it solves. Text might be misspelt, arrows misdirected and pathways altered. More importantly, the resulting image is usually flat (that is, the text, images and background are merged together), making it mostly uneditable. For diagrams in research publications, if a reviewer later asks you to alter it, you might have to start from scratch.

A better option is to ask a multimodal language model — for example, Google’s Gemini — to turn your idea into a structured diagram format, such as Draw.io-compatible XML or Mermaid syntax. The output can then be imported into a diagram editor, in which every box, label and connector remains editable.

In this workflow, AI is less an illustrator than a compiler: a programming tool that translates human-readable instructions into code that a computer can run. My sketch is the source, and Draw.io XML is the output.

Focus first on the structure of your figure. I roughly sketch the important nodes, branches and connections without worrying about visual polish. For a clinical study, these might include eligibility criteria, treatment groups and follow-up visits. For a laboratory workflow, they might represent experimental stages or decision points.

The key is to make the relationships clear. What box comes first? Where does the pathway split? Which arrow connects to which endpoint? If the logic is ambiguous to a human reader, it will be ambiguous to the AI model, too.

Once the sketch is complete, I photograph it, upload the image to a vision-enabled language model and provide a detailed prompt. For instance:

“Recreate the uploaded hand-drawn figure as a clean, editable academic flowchart in Draw.io-compatible XML format. Preserve the original structure as faithfully as possible, including box positions, arrows, dashed connectors, side boxes, branching pattern, and text content. This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task. Use a plain white background, thin dark slate-grey borders, white box fills, thin connector lines, clean sans-serif text, and no shadows, gradients, or decorative elements. Make it publication-quality while keeping it recognizably the same diagram.”

The instruction “This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task” is crucial. Scientific diagrams are not the place for creative completion. I want the model to reconstruct my structure, not improve it on my behalf.

Note also that this prompt indicates what the model should not change. I explicitly ask it to preserve wording, branching relationships and directionality. If the diagram contains important numbers, doses or time points, I check each one manually.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03513-1

Exactly how much Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) headroom do Manchester United have to back Mauricio Pochettino in the January transfer window?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino has barely unpacked his bags at Old Trafford, but it's already abundantly clear Manchester United need to back their new head coach in January.

Following a disappointing start to the campaign and the arrival of a new regulatory era in English football, the club’s latest financial results offer a clear picture as to how much room INEOS actually have to manoeuvre.

Man United’s most recent full-year accounts, covering the 12-month period to 30 June, 2026, which were published in September, paints a picture of cost-cutting paired with historically strong commercial standing.

Despite having no European football last season, Man United posted record revenue of £677.6 million while trimming wages for a third consecutive year to £302.0m.

Although previous recruitment pushed player amortisation to £211.8m and left a net loss of £43.0m after finance costs, £47.0m in player-sale profits kept the underlying business moving forward.

Even more telling are Man United’s first-quarter results for 2026/27, released on November 19.

With Champions League football back at Old Trafford, quarterly revenue rose 4.1 per cent to £146.1m, and the club are predicted to earn £740m and £760m annually.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Quarterly player amortisation fell by almost 15 per cent following summer exits and Casemiro’s contract expiry, while another £20.7m was banked in player-disposal profits.

This summer, the Premier League replaced Profitability and Sustainability Rules (PSR) with its new Squad Cost Ratio (SCR) system. Under SCR, clubs’ on-pitch spending - which comprises first-team player and head coach wages, transfer amortisation, and agent fees, while excluding non-playing staff, academy and women’s team costs - is capped at 85 per cent of football revenue plus net profit on player sales.

There is even a 30 per cent multi-year buffer up to a 115 per cent ‘Red Threshold’ before points deductions apply. However, because Man United are competing in the Champions League, they must simultaneously adhere to UEFA’s stricter 70 per cent squad cost limit ahead of the March 1 compliance checkpoint.

Therefore, Pochettino has far more breathing room in the transfer market than naysayers might suggest.

Taking the £750m midpoint of Man United’s expected 2026/27 revenue and adding roughly £45m - which is an average of player-trading profits over recent years - that gives an adjusted revenue figure of £795m.

Under the Premier League’s 85 per cent threshold, Man United could carry £675.8m in annual squad costs. Under UEFA’s tighter 70 per cent ceiling, their limit sits at £556.5m.

Remove non-playing staff from total wages and Man United’s first-team player and coaching bill sits near £255m. Add £186.4m in annualised amortisation and roughly £35m in agents’ fees, and total squad costs land around £476.4m - roughly 60 per cent of adjusted revenue.

That leaves roughly £80m in annual squad-cost headroom beneath UEFA’s 70 per cent cap - and nearly £200m domestically.

This means Man United could comfortably sanction £120m to £150m in winter transfer spending. That said, their borrowing position and existing credit facility could yet prove to be a handbrake on any January rebuild, but from a purely regulatory standpoint, Man United's transfer expenditure picture is a rosy one.

#845. Joshua Zirkzee urges Manchester United to look beyond refereeing decisions after Sporting draw

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The striker acknowledged that several contentious decisions went against Manchester United in Lisbon

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Joshua Zirkzee insisted Manchester United must focus on their own performance rather than pointing fingers at controversial refereeing following their 2-2 Champions League draw against Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday night.

The tie in Lisbon was marked by a series of contentious calls from Polish match official Szymon Marciniak, prompting former United captain and BBC Radio 5 Live pundit Ashley Young to describe the officiating as "a disgrace".

Marciniak disallowed Amad Diallo’s first-half equaliser by blowing his whistle before the ball hit the back of an empty net, having wrongly judged Youri Tielemans to have fouled Goncalo Inacio in the buildup.

The United midfielder’s frustration over the booking was compounded when he received a second yellow card in the closing stages of the match.

The referee also ruled out a late winner for United after being directed to the pitchside monitor, deciding goalkeeper Kaique Pereira had been fouled by Patrick Dorgu.

However, speaking in a post-match interview with MUTV, Zirkzee said: "In my opinion, there were definitely some key decisions there that didn’t really favour us.

"We shouldn’t look at the referee, we should look at ourselves instead, but it definitely has an impact on us, you can’t deny that.

"But the team that we have, we should come here and not look at the ref and make sure that we get the win, regardless of the decisions that he makes."

Marciniak had also awarded Sporting a dubious first-half penalty after Lisandro Martinez made slight contact with Geny Catamo, though Senne Lammens saved the effort.

"Obviously, we did come here to win, so in a way, we’ve got some positives to take," Zirkzee said.

"But with our recent form, of course, we’re disappointed to not win. Some positives to take, we’ve just got to keep moving forward, keep going together, keep putting in the work and move on to the next game."

Making his first start of the campaign, Zirkzee expressed his gratitude to the supporters, adding: "I’m very happy. Every game you play for this club is an honour.

"I’ve been here for some time and it’s been a while since I started a game, so I’m very happy, I just wish we could have got a win.

"For where we’re standing at right now, to have a fanbase like that is just incredible.

"All we can do is get up the next day and make sure the next time they travel with us and the next time they watch our game, we repay it, so that’s all we can do for now."

United, who sit 19th in the Champions League standings, fell behind at Estadio Jose Alvalade to a Luis Suarez spot-kick. They responded through Bruno Fernandes’ double – the first coming from the penalty spot – before Suarez seized on a late error from Lammens to secure a draw.

Mauricio Pochettino will now aim for his first win in charge of United when they host Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday.

Chelsea are preparing for life after Xabi Alonso, following a 4-1 thumping at home to Leeds United.

That's according to one report, which states that despite hiring the Basque boss over the summer and backing him heavily with big signings, such as Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers, the Blues are looking at the next man to take charge.

With Chelsea having lost three of the last five, a title challenge has turned into a battle for Europe, with the manager now under threat.

After a strong start to the season, Chelsea have tapered off, with Alonso facing several of the same problems that predecessors Liam Rosenior and Enzo Fernandez encountered during their Stamford Bridge stints.

Despite being given the title of 'manager' rather than 'head coach' – and thus wielding a little more power in recruitment – the club are still hampered by injuries, with the defence looking shakier than ever.

TEAMtalk have reported that despite Alonso's four-year deal, former Blues midfielder Cesc Fabregas is “right at the top of the list” to replace his former international colleague in the hot seat.

Como boss Fabregas won two league titles in West London and has masterminded an incredibly impressive surge towards the top in Italian football, with a recent Champions League thumping over Manchester United shocking Europe.

The report states that the Spaniard “would not be willing to take the Chelsea job in the middle of the season” – while transfer influencer Fabrizio Romano claimed recently that ownership BlueCo are backing Alonso for now.

“The message I’m getting is a very clear message around Xabi Alonso – Chelsea trust their manager,” the Italian said on his YouTube channel.

“Chelsea owners, Chelsea directors, Chelsea as a club go in the same direction and they believe in Alonso. They trust Alonso. They want to give time to Alonso.

Newcastle United and head coach Matthias Jaissle could reunite with a former striker, according to reports

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Newcastle are being tipped to solve their goalscoring issues this winter with a move to bring Ivan Toney back to St James’ Park.

It is a transfer which would reunite the England international with former boss Matthias Jaissle, with whom he worked at current club Al-Ahli.

Finding the back of the net has proved a major headache for Jaissle since taking the reins on Tyneside and following a summer exodus that stripped the Magpies of their spine, none of Newcastle’s current central striking options have managed to nail down a starting spot in his team.

Will Osula and Yoane Wissa have mustered just a single league goal apiece so far this campaign, while Matias Fernandez-Pardo is still waiting to open his account. Without a reliable penalty-box presence, Jaissle’s side have lacked a cutting edge in the final third.

Toney thrived under Jaissle during their time together in Saudi Arabia. The former Brentford frontman has been expectedly prolific in the Middle East, netting 87 times in 110 appearances across all competitions.

Any transfer negotiations may even be smoothed over by shared ownership links, as both Al-Ahli and Newcastle are majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Despite his form in the Saudi Pro League, Toney has slipped down the international pecking order and missed out on recent England squads, a setback that is expected to spark a push for a Premier League return in the New Year.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Speaking on the Everything is Black and White Podcast, The Chronicle’s chief Newcastle reporter Lee Ryder suggested the 30-year-old will be chomping at the bit to head back to English football.

A switch to St James’ Park would see Toney return to the club he departed almost a decade ago. Newcastle originally signed the striker from Northampton Town over in 2015, but made just two Premier League outings before being sent out on a series of loans. Spells at Barnsley, Shrewsbury, Scunthorpe and Wigan followed, before he was eventually sold to Peterborough United in 2018.

Having since proved his top-flight pedigree at Brentford, Toney would bring additional physicality and an aptitude for finishing that Newcastle are presently missing.

#842. Wirtz follows rich Liverpool heritage with star showing in win over Brugge

It had to be this way. Liverpool No 7s have historically defined matches against Club Brugge, so it was entirely appropriate that Florian Wirtz preserved that rich heritage.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

On another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

The idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the footballing landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.

Alexander Isak finds the back of the net to give Liverpool the lead against Club Brugge! 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/vZbiHKkpiy

“He is in a great moment,” Andoni Iraola, Liverpool’s head coach, said of his striker. “When the team is playing well and getting good results everyone looks better. In the second half we defended lower and knew there would be space to exploit. In one of those moments, he killed the game.”

Liverpool are not perfect, by any means, but the closer you watch them, the more obvious it is that they are grasping what Iraola wants. They will be a good team when it does click, but these are just the first steps of the journey. The first half proved it.

Some moves broke down with a misplaced pass and Brugge were often let off the hook when they were guilty of over-elaboration. Iraola wants Liverpool to be ruthless, but his mood soured for a period, not least when Victor Muñoz injured his knee in an incident when he was trying to win back possession.

“A knock on the knee and we have to test it,” Iraola said. “That was the worst part of the night. It is very early to tell but it was very painful at that moment. He was better after the game.”

So, too, was Iraola, who was especially pleased that Liverpool recorded their first Champions League clean sheet of the season and, in the process, stopped Brugge – who had scored in 19 consecutive games – from finding a way through.

There were several reasons this was the case: Jérémy Jacquet, for instance, never put a foot wrong – what a smart signing he has proved to be. He more than did his bit to retain order in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, who was given the chance to catch his breath before the Merseyside derby.

It was tough for Liverpool in the second period, as Brugge attacked the end of the stadium where their noisy ultras created a cacophony. Yet they handled the situation well, even if Iraola looked ready to combust at one stage, receiving a yellow card for protesting too much to the officials.

“I saw the referee beforehand, I know him from Spain and I knew this was coming,” Iraola said.

Perhaps his ire was fuelled by Liverpool squandering a fabulous chance on the hour to kill things off. A move that featured Wirtz and Isak exchanging passes with pinball precision ended with Szoboszlai bearing down on Sommer, but his shot was too close to the veteran.

He had to score and the grimace that followed had nothing to do with heavy strapping the Hungarian had on supporting his right knee. That miss would have been exacerbated in the 69th minute had Alisson Becker not made a superb save to deny Félix Lemaréchal, plunging to avert the danger.

Liverpool have travelled over to Belgium to take on Club Brugge on matchday five in the Champions League. These sides have met competitively three times before and they have all come in finals, resulting in famous nights for Liverpool. In 1976, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 4-3 on aggregate across two legs to win the Uefa Cup. Then, Kenny Dalglish scored the only goal of the game at Wembley back in May 1978 as Liverpool won the European Cup for the second straight season, becoming the first English side to do so.

Liverpool, who have won 13 of their previous 17 matches against Belgian sides, won their first three Champions League games, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal but lost 3-2 away at Fenerbahce on matchday four despite leading twice in that game. After tonight’s game in Belgium, Liverpool’s remaining games in the Champions League are against Porto, Inter Milan and Lens. Andoni Iraola’s side come into this game with a spring in their step after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

“A win [against Manchester United on Sunday] is always great but you do not have time to celebrate with this schedule,” Iraola said. “By Monday, we were already watching analysis of Club Brugge. I have enjoyed analysing them [Brugge], they are very energetic and have had an incredible run of games. I think we will have to be at a very good level, otherwise it is going to be very difficult. They have players who can make the difference and obviously we do as well, so I expect quite an open game. We are both aggressive, both want to press, there will be spaces and hopefully we can win the one-vs-one battles.”

Club Brugge have made a strong start to this season’s Champions League; after losing their first game to Aston Villa, they have since won their next three, including wins over Inter Milan, Lens and PSV. That puts them on the same number of points as Liverpool and are just one place behind. In the Belgian Pro League at the weekend, they thrashed Mechelen 5-1 and they sit second in the Belgian top flight, one point behind Union SG.

“I am proud of the players and what they have achieved against Aston Villa, Inter, Lens and PSV,” Club Brugge boss Ivan Leko said. “We know we should be grateful to be here, but we really want to try to show that Belgian football is fun to watch and we can win matches. I am proud, but I know we are a big club. You are only as good as your last match. We know what happened in the past, so there is also a nice connection between both clubs and the supporters. It is a special fixture to play, but we are not here just to enjoy the Champions League; we want to win and that is what we are going to try to do tomorrow [tonight].”

#841. Liverpool v Man Utd referee made ‘obvious error’ sending off Leny Yoro as written reasons published

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Man Utd defender’s suspension has been overturned, with an independent regulatory commission unanimously concluding that Referee Sam Barrott’s decision was wrong

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Referee Sam Barrott made an “obvious error” by giving Manchester United defender Leny Yoro a red card against Liverpool, an independent regulatory commission unanimously concluded.

Yoro was given his marching orders when he hauled down Swedish striker Alexander Isak in the opening stages of last Sunday’s fiery match at Anfield.

Debate raged over Isak’s touch and whether goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have collected the ball had Yoro not made contact.

Even referees’ chief Howard Webb concluded that the call was “certainly not clearly wrong”, but then Manchester United appealed to the Football Association for wrongful dismissal and successfully removed his one-match ban on Tuesday.

The three-person panel’s written reasons were published on Thursday and stated: “The commission members were unanimous that, taking the foul committed by LY (Yoro) out of the scenario, AI (Isak) would not have had an obvious goalscoring opportunity.

“Despite the fact that AI had reached the ball initially, his touch was heavy to the extent that he had in fact lost control of the ball – that control had, in effect, passed to the advancing MUFC goalkeeper who in the view of the commission would have been able to gather or smother the ball before AI could get to it and shoot at goal.

“To the mind of the commission, the referee had made an ‘obvious error’ in deciding that AI (Isak) would have had an obvious goalscoring opportunity.”

Webb, the chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref, told the Match Officials: Mic’d Up programme which aired on Tuesday, shortly after confirmation the ban had been removed: “There’s a question mark I guess around whether or not he (Isak) would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

“The VAR checks to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn’t.

“I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it’s a little bit debatable. (It’s) certainly not clearly wrong.”

The FA’s independent panel, which was made up of former Blackburn and Middlesbrough winger Stuart Ripley, former Sheffield United and Notts County forward Tony Agana and ex-Walsall goalkeeper Mick Kearns, disagreed.

The reasons confirm that United submitted technical information to the panel which concluded Isak would have been, at best, 1.8 metres short of the ball even if Yoro had not made the challenge.

The reasons state that the commission “had no way of testing the validity of this analysis undertaken by the club and as such the evidence was viewed with caution and allocated weight accordingly”.

To add to the confusion, the Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel is reported by the Daily Mail to have backed Barrott’s call and the decision of the VAR John Brooks not to recommend a review.

The five-person KMI Panel is comprised of three former players and coaches, one Premier League representative and one from Pro Ref, and its findings for the match week where the incident occurred are due to be published on December 2.

Pro Ref declined to comment on the Mail story, or on the commission’s findings. Manchester United have been approached for comment.

The reasons revealed that United also submitted a video of a challenge by Brighton’s Pascal Struijk on Wilson Isidor of Sunderland last month. Struijk was shown a red card after the VAR recommended a review for denial of an obvious goalscoring opportunity. Struijk’s suspension was removed after an appeal to the FA by Brighton.

The removal of the ban means Yoro is free to face Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday.

United encountered further refereeing controversy in their 2-2 Champions League draw away to Sporting in Lisbon on Wednesday night.

The Red Devils had a first-half goal disallowed after Polish referee Szymon Marciniak blew for what looked at best a very soft-looking foul by Youri Tielemans before Amad Diallo had put the ball in the net. They then had a winner ruled out when VAR recommended a review for what was deemed to be a foul by United’s Patrick Dorgu on Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, though the Brazilian appeared to have fumbled into his own net before the Dorgu challenge came in.

To rub salt into their wounds, Tielemans – who was booked for the challenge that led to the Diallo goal being disallowed – was then shown a second yellow in injury time.

#840. Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.
