#789. Chelsea Q&A: Are Blues in crisis? What next for Fofana after viral interview?

Your questions answered by Sky Sports News' James Savundra on Chelsea's season, with Blues having lost three of last four in Premier League; Wesley Fofana’s unauthorised interview, the absences of Danny Welbeck and Estevao, and January transfer plans all addressed

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.

As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Here, Savundra addresses Fofana's future, Joao Pedro's injury, transfer plans and much more...

Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.

James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.

Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?

James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.

Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.

You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?

The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso of Wesley Fofana: "We have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate. He has apologised. He knows it wasn't the right moment. The content wasn't right. "We are here to take things seriously and he said it wouldn't be repeated. We know it's something we don't want and they are not going to be repeated."

Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.

James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.

It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.

The fact that Xabi Alonso opted for a false nine in three matches prior to Leeds would suggest he believes there are shortcomings in both Emegha and Welbeck's games. It feels more likely that Chelsea will revisit the forward line next summer.

JD: How has Joao Pedro's injury affected how Chelsea has been playing as an overall team, and how has Xabi Alonso had to adapt to it?

James says: The stats are undeniable. Since the start of last season, Chelsea average 1.8 goals per game when Joao Pedro plays, compared to 0.6 when he doesn't. It's quite staggering the difference that the Brazilian seems to make.

Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers look far more potent when they are playing off him. Danny Welbeck initially started in his absence at Brentford. However, he had virtually no impact and appears to have fallen down the pecking order.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

Xabi Alonso doesn't tend to give much away but he has described Emegha as being a player with "special" qualities. There's clearly an adaptation period required and Emegha missed a lot of football last season due to injury.

He was also signed prior to Alonso's arrival so it was very much a club signing. Chelsea's season has been derailed by the absence of key players such as Reece James, Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo.

Alonso needs his big players to step up to ensure they can cope with the casualties - albeit to really key players.

Adam: Why does Alonso not start Welbeck whilst Joao Pedro is injured? Given his experience?

James says: The treatment of Welbeck has been puzzling. He performed really well in the opening two Carabao Cup matches of the season but has featured sparingly since the Brentford defeat.

It was interesting to see how late he was brought on against Tottenham despite Chelsea's need to turn the tide. The 36-year-old (happy birthday today, Danny!) clearly cannot get around the pitch with the same intensity and speed he did when he broke through at Manchester United but that was obvious when he was signed.

Alonso has deflected when asked about Welbeck's lack of minutes but perhaps his inability to press with intensity is one of the main reasons behind him spending more time on the bench than on the pitch.

He's still got a brilliant goalscoring touch - as seen last season at Brighton. He may benefit from more opportunities during a busy December period.

Tim: Should Chelsea be starting Estevao more often? If not, then what should we do with him? Where could we send him on loan if we can't guarantee minutes?

James says: Estevao has only started twice this season - both times at home. He made a huge impact on the pitch and on the supporters when he started in the win against Manchester United. His lack of physical robustness and defensive acumen would appear to be why Xabi Alonso has used him so sparingly.

However, I don't think his lack of minutes is going to be sustainable long-term. There's an argument given Cole Palmer's drop off that Estevao should get an opportunity at No 10. Chelsea see Estevao as one of their "untouchable" players and they would be extremely reluctant to let him leave.

I asked Alonso last month about whether a loan could be an option in January. The Spaniard said that it had not been discussed. Something is going to have to give at some point.

Estevao is still a teenager so has lots of learning and development left. However, he would be a key player for many of the top clubs in Europe.

He needs to find a way to force his way into Alonso's plans. A January departure is very unlikely but conversations will need to take place in the summer if his lack of football continues.

Saying that, if Chelsea do qualify for Europe next season then there should be more opportunities.

Sam: Which manager is in more need of a win on Friday, Oliver Glasner or Alonso?

James says: Both clubs feel like they are in very similar situations right now. Both signing managers to deliver a cultural reboot and sustained success. Yet both have had challenging starts.

I was at Glasner's press conference on Thursday and he spoke about lengthy conversations he had with the club owner earlier this week about January transfers and standards. Forest gave him an extremely lucrative contract and will want to give him as much time as they can.

However, given they have had five managers in the space of a year, it's difficult to predict anything at Forest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Chelsea have full confidence in Xabi Alonso but home defeats against Spurs and Leeds have really harmed his approval ratings amongst supporters.

It would feel like a crisis if Chelsea lost three league matches on the bounce, so I would say Alonso needs a win just a little bit more than Glasner.

If Forest can create an atmosphere at the City Ground similar to their win against Manchester City then Chelsea will really be tested. Liam Delap will be desperate to prove a point.

It might get worse before it gets better for Manchester City fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

Manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

Man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

Charles Leclerc has strongly denied suggestions he has a No 1 driver clause in his Ferrari contract.

The Monegasque, who has been with the team since 2019 and signed an extended deal earlier this year, was speaking ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix as both he and Lewis Hamilton faced the media again four days on from their latest clash at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing a collision as he attempted to overtake Hamilton for sixth place in Las Vegas, with the incident also earning him severe criticism from Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur.

The Las Vegas collision came just three weeks after a fierce battle between the team-mates - with Hamilton running first and Leclerc second - on the opening lap in Mexico City cost Ferrari a likely one-two, with clear-the-air discussions required after Red Bull's Max Verstappen won that race.

Vasseur has hitherto played down the need to impose strict, pre-determined rules of engagement on his drivers to avoid future repeats. There had subsequently been speculation that, perhaps, there were contractual reasons on Leclerc's side preventing the team from formally intervening in this way.

But offered the chance on Thursday to address claims about the presence of a so-called 'No 1 driver' clause in his deal, Leclerc said: "I normally never disclose what I have in my contract, but I think this one is an important one to speak about.

"And I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.

George Russell admits feud with Max Verstappen is 'avoidable' and 'unnecessary' ahead of Qatar Grand Prix

Qatar GP: Explaining 2026 tyre-limit rule and what impact it will have on F1 race weekend at Lusail International Circuit

Qatar GP 2026: Dates, schedule, weather, UK start time and how to watch or stream F1 race at Lusail International Circuit live on Sky Sports

"It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc bore the brunt of Vasseur's post-race criticism last Sunday and, asked if he agreed with the Frenchman that the crash with Hamilton had indeed been "unacceptable", replied: "That it is unacceptable? Of course.

"As a team, we cannot afford to clash between team-mates and I think that is very clear for everyone. For the clash in particular of Las Vegas, as I said, I took responsibility.

"I think there's just tension around, that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future.

"That's all I'm looking for. But yeah, I do agree. It's unacceptable that both Ferrari clash together, of course."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Vasseur had promised further talks with his drivers following the race in Vegas, having insisted the clashes between the pair "cannot continue".

The drivers confirmed on Thursday that talks had taken place, with both the team principal and among themselves, with Hamilton saying they had been "good discussions" and "positive".

Neither driver said they would elaborate on the specifics of what was discussed, with Leclerc stating in the official FIA news conference that he "cannot disclose" what possible "solutions" were agreed to avoid future repeats or whether any restrictions were in place for the season's final two rounds.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton later confirmed they remained free to race each other this weekend in Qatar

"We're still free to race, and I think that's the ultimate goal of being here. We want to race, right?" said Hamilton to Sky Sports F1.

"Of course, we don't want what happened last week to ever happen, so we communicate. Charles and I had a good sit down earlier on and had our chat, and I I think moving forwards we can be fine.

"We literally focus on racing hard and fair, and continue to try and enjoy it. We do enjoy racing together, and we do have a really good relationship.

"It's obviously intense in the background, well on the outside, it seems a lot more intense than it really is inside."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Hamilton has previously called for the team to adopt clearer guidelines on how he and Leclerc are able to race each other but, speaking on Thursday, said it was Vasseur's final call to make.

"That's for Fred to decide ultimately," he said. "I made my point clear already about them.

"So yeah, there's not really much more to say on it really. I said my piece before and and my point hasn't really changed."

Leclerc and Hamilton are in their second season as Ferrari team-mates and will at least spend one more year in tandem in 2027, with the potential for more.

Asked if he thought they could move forward in harmony, Hamilton said: "I do. We're going to figure it out.

"We're team-mates at the end of the day and we do always learn from these experiences whilst maybe it doesn't necessarily look like it.

"There will be learnings that we take from this difficult period, and I still believe in everything we're building and working towards in the background.

"I came here with the goal of taking Ferrari back to the top and it has been a massively challenging season but it's so easy to look at the negatives but I like to look at the positives this year."

Ferrari can clinch the runner-up position to world champions Mercedes this weekend in Qatar and Hamilton added: "We are fighting for second in the Constructors' Championship, we have had wins, I think we've had the best car chassis-wise particularly this year and that's down to all the amazing people back at the factory who have worked and brought upgrades. I am so proud of them.

"Did we have the straight-line speed? No. That's something we are working towards for next year. If we are able to galvanise and improve on that section, we're going to be mighty next year in my view.

"I'm just trying to look at the positives, I think everyone seems to be focusing always on the negatives, which is obviously the easiest thing to do in life. But I try to remember the positives, and we've really done some amazing things this year together."

Hamilton added: "I like to think that we are stronger. I think that if everything was just great all the time I don't think you learn anything.

"When you're winning all the time as well, you don't learn a lot through that. You learn really through the hardest times, and these are the definitely very, very challenging times for Fred, for Charles and I, but these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together, through conversation, communicating and having those sit-downs.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leclerc believes his off-track relationship with Hamilton is "really strong" and they now needed to find a workable way forward when racing each other on track.

"We're just really very much focused on trying to find a solution that works," said Leclerc.

"Particularly because I really believe we are in a good momentum and if next year we are to be in a position of fighting for the championship, it's even more so important to find the right solution for both of us to bring Ferrari back to the top.

"At the end of the day, we are two, one in each car, and we need to make sure that things just work out. At the moment, it's not working.

"Then, of course, I can take the blame from one episode and whatever. That doesn't really matter. It's just important that we find a compromise and a solution that works for both."

Arsenal could lose a first-team defender who has fallen out of favour with manager Mikel Arteta.

The Gunners boast arguably the best backline in Europe at the moment, having conceded the fewest goals in the Premier League this term (just seven), and goalkeeper David Raya has already kept seven clean sheets in 11 fixtures.

Part of Arsenal's strength at the back is in their depth – but that could be seriously impacted with interest in a star who hasn't been getting in the team as much of late.

Following a back injury at the 2026 World Cup to William Saliba, the Gunners moved to bring in quality cover in the shape of England international Ezri Konsa.

Konsa has been an instant hit at the Emirates Stadium, and with Arteta now boasting eight senior players competing for places – Konsa, Saliba, Gabriel and Cristhian Mosquera in the centre, with full-backs Jurrien Timber, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie all capable in the middle, too – the problem is giving each of them playing time.

#783. Alan Bersten Speaks Out After Helping Ezra Frech When His Leg Fell Off

Dancing With the Stars pro Alan Bersten shared his reaction to Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach's win after he helped the duo when Frech's prosthetic leg flew off mid-dance.

Alan Bersten deserves the Mirrorball for best backup dancer.

The Dancing With the Stars pro proved he was Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach’s secret weapon during the Nov. 24 finale while performing during their freestyle routine to Linkin’ Park’s “Numb.” When the Paralympian’s prosthetic leg accidentally fell off mid-show, Bersten quickly grabbed the device and held it for safekeeping until Karagach could give it to Frech to reattach during the song. Plus, Bersten was locked into the choreography and didn’t even miss his cue to tear off Frech’s rip-away clothing.

Following Frech and Karagach’s win, Bersten shared how honored he was to have taken part in the dance alongside the duo.

“I just want to take a second and congratulate Ezra and Daniella,” he said in a Nov. 25 TikTok. “Ezra, your resilience and your composure and your courage is so inspiring.”

The 32-year-old—who was eliminated during week two alongside pro partner Giada De Laurentiis—added that the moment Frech reattached his leg mid-dance was one that “transcends Dancing with the Stars.”

“It's a moment that will live on forever,” he said. “And I hope you are so proud of yourself, Daniella. You've created something so magical. Congratulations, you guys.”

Karagach thanked her fellow pro for not only grabbing the prosthetic when it fell, but also for clearing away Frech’s tearaway suit from the stage so it wouldn’t get in their way.

“The way @alanbersten slid me that leg and made sure Ezra's rip away was cleared was true professionalism at its finest,” the 33-year-old posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 24. “Grateful you had our backs. Can't thank you enough.”

The moment was also one that Frech himself would never forget as he recounted what was going through his mind the moment his prosthetic flew off.

“The leg just wasn't on correctly, and I felt it,” the 21-year-old told Variety following the episode. “Sometimes it'll readjust and I'll be okay. And so, as I was running up the steps, I'm like, ‘There's a 50 percent chance my leg will resuction and I'll be OK.’ And that wasn't the case.”

And while he was tempted to do the entire routine on one leg, he recalled hearing Karagach say, “‘Put your leg on,’ and I was like, ‘Yes, OK, yeah, good idea. I'll put it on right now.’”

Frech was able to reattach the limb before the duo gracefully jumped back into their routine, with Karagach explaining she quickly realized there was no other place in the dance that he could have taken a moment to reattach it.

“Nothing's better than him just clicking on his leg properly and continuing on with the dance,” she said. “I was like, ‘This is our only shot to do that.’”

Still, with all the adrenaline coursing through him, Frech actually had trouble remembering how exactly he got his prosthetic back.

“Did somebody give me the leg? Because I blacked out,” he asked aloud, to which Karagach confirmed she gave it to him. “You gave me the leg? Really?”

And as expected, the routine left its mark on the series, with judge Derek Hough telling the dancing duo, “This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show. What you did tonight was forever. Kids will look up to you and see what's possible."

#781. What Is Airing on NBC Instead of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade 2026

After the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was interrupted for the fourth time since its debut in 1924, NBC has shared what will be broadcast in its place for 2026.

While it's too late for a Thanksgiving miracle, NBC does have a back-up plan for the Macy's Parade.

Although the New York weather forecast is in fact raining on its parade—with severe wind and rain forcing the 2026 Macy's Day Parade to move from Thursday to Saturday—the network revealed what will air in its place on Nov. 26.

In lieu of the scheduled program, NBC will re-air last year's show at 8 a.m. in all time zones, a spokesperson from the network told E! News in a Nov. 25 statement. And lucky for viewers, given the unforgettable moments of 2025, the second broadcast is sure to make for spectacular leftovers.

The affair began with Wicked star Cynthia Erivo singing a rendition of "Feeling Good" by Nina Simone. From there, the day included performances by Busta Rhymes, Teyana Taylor and Mr. Fantasy—who fans believe is the stage persona of Riverdale actor KJ Apa. And the parade was not complete without an appearance by the Radio City Rockettes—who have been a highlight of the show since 1957—as well as Santa Claus.

As news broke that fans whose Thanksgiving tradition involves spending the afternoon with anchors Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker should expect something different this year, the broadcaster explained the decision was made in the interest of safety.

"Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided," the NBC representative said. "In the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28. More details to follow."

And due to the pivot, some performers may not stay on the 2026 lineup, according to NBC News, as shared by reporter Jesse Kirsch.

"The parade on Saturday may not include everyone who was supposed to be in it," Kirsch said. "I just spoke with the director of one of the bands. He told me they've got flights, they've got hotel rooms that are set in stone, and it's unclear if they would be able to rearrange things."

Terry Venables arrived at Middlesbrough in 2000 to work alongside manager Bryan Robson in an unconventional setup

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.

The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

Schwarzer had reason to worry about the potential for awkwardness when Venables was appointed to work alongside Bryan Robson at the Riverside in December 2000, tasked with helping Middlesbrough to beat the drop.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: “I was worried when Terry came in, because his previous job had been manager of Australia.

“I’d just joined Middlesbrough when we had that League Cup semi-final at the same time as an Australia call-up.

"Terry had made it clear that if he called you up, he expected you to be there

"Bryan Robson asked him if I could stay because it was one of the biggest games in Middlesbrough’s history.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Terry initially agreed, then three days beforehand called and said I had to choose. I told him I’d made a commitment to my club. He didn’t pick me again, including for the World Cup play-off against Iran.

“When he arrived at Middlesbrough, I wondered if there might be a problem. To his credit, he was brilliant. He basically said 'These things happen, let’s move on'."

Instead of allowing the dispute to linger, Schwarzer says Venables did a fantastic job of working out how to get Middlesbrough back in form

He said: “He made a huge impact at Middlesbrough. He spoke to everyone about what they thought was going wrong, then made his own mind up about how to address it.

“Terry was exceptional at not undermining Bryan. Robbo was still at the front of things but had this incredible coach to learn from. If Terry hadn’t come in, we would have been relegated.”

Boro eventually finished the 2000-01 Premier League season in 14th, well clear of the drop.

Liverpool are beginning to see the very best of Florian Wirtz if recent form is anything to go by

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

Supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

His end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

So, what has initiated the turnaround? New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

Since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her new long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

“Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she said. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

“To be part of that journey is really special.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

"I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she said.

"I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

"You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get."

The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

#776. Gukesh to defend chess crown against rising star Sindarov

As the World Chess championship gets underway, it's no coincidence that the titleholder, Gukesh Dommaraju, and his challenger, Jakhovir Sindarov, are both from Asia.

When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.

"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he said.

Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

Gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.

Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.

"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov said.

Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.

"He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.

"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot."

By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.

"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.

"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift."

While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

Now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.

"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson said.

Another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad."

#775. Saving Nepal’s wild orchids — in photos

Prized for their ornamental and medicinal value, hundreds of orchids are illegally harvested and sold each year. Now, conservationist Reshu Bashyal is leading an effort to protect them.

Words by Saugat Bolakhe and photos by CJ Karki

A couple of hours drive from Kathmandu, in the hills near Chitlang village in central Nepal, a group of locals and forest officials gather in a dense subtropical woodland. Beneath a canopy of pines, Himalayan chestnuts and Nepalese alders, the group listens as wildlife conservationist Reshu Bashyal guides them through a questionnaire designed to document the signs of poaching.

Bashyal refers to this team as a taskforce — one on the hunt for illegal activity. But instead of focusing on animals, as many conservation projects do, the group’s objective is to protect flora, specifically orchids. These flowering plants are harvested and sold across Nepal’s borders.

The flowers are prized for their ornamental value, but they are also used in traditional medicines, including Chinese, Tibetan and Ayurveda healing products.

Multiple parts of the plant, including the stem and fruit, can also be used as ingredients. “It’s as if these plants have some magical properties about them,” Bashyal says.

Nepal has more than 500 orchid species, many of which are heavily harvested. Between 2008 and 2016, the country legally exported more than 47,000 kilograms of wild-collected orchids. However, discrepancies exist between Nepal’s export data and those of its trading partners, arising from issues such as mismatched and unreported trade amounts and species being sold under different names.

The trade in animal and plant species is regulated mostly under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) agreement, which is designed to protect wildlife from exploitation. Although Nepal joined the convention more than 50 years ago, it did not introduce legislation to implement CITES until 2017.

The orchid Dendrobium longicornu is sought after for its black-haired canes and fragrant white and orange blooms.

The orchid Dendrobium longicornu is sought after for its black-haired canes and fragrant white and orange blooms.

All but two species of orchid in Nepal are now listed in CITES Appendix II, which includes species that are not currently threatened with extinction but could be if their trade is not regulated. The government must create a management plan and a formal assessment to confirm that harvesting a species for trade won’t harm the survival of the wild population. “We haven’t prepared such a management plan for any orchid species yet. So, their trade is still considered illegal here,” Bashyal adds. Violation of the CITES Act can lead to a fine of up to 100,000 Nepalese rupees (US$660), one year in prison, or both.

Bashyal started researching orchids in 2018, when conservation fieldwork revealed the extent of harvesting and trade of the plants.

Bashyal started researching orchids in 2018, when conservation fieldwork revealed the extent of harvesting and trade of the plants.

Bashyal demonstrates a survey technique to a member of her team.

Bashyal demonstrates a survey technique to a member of her team.

Bashyal (right) and a team from the non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal have partnered with forest officials and local community members to form an anti-poaching taskforce.

Bashyal (right) and a team from the non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal have partnered with forest officials and local community members to form an anti-poaching taskforce.

Bashyal first became involved in orchid research by chance. In 2018, while working on a conifer tree conservation project for non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal in Kathmandu, she visited several regional sites across the country and was often approached by people asking about the demand for orchids in the city. When her team investigated further, it realized that many people living in the villages were harvesting or actively trading the plants.

This illegal trading was often overlooked by authorities, according to Bashyal. Before suggesting a way to stop it, the team had to understand the market — specifically which species were being taken, their conservation status and how the supply chain operated. To do this, it visited orchid trading hubs across Nepal and spoke to harvesters, traders and enforcement officials.

The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife.

The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife.

“The local people provide information on where orchids are harvested, moved, gathered and how much they sold orchids for,” she says. During these visits, the team shared its research and spoke about the importance of conservation, which was well received, she says. “After all, an unsustainable harvesting of the orchids severely threatens local livelihood and income,” she adds.

Bashyal’s team at Greenhood Nepal learnt that several orchid species, including Satyrium nepalense and Pleione praecox, are harvested in large quantities for their medicinal value. Overharvesting an orchid species that is in decline can easily lead to its extinction in the wild, which makes understanding a species’ population and distribution crucial for creating sustainable harvesting practices.

After the field trips, Bashyal’s team created a series of policy briefs, drafted conservation frameworks and started the anti-poaching taskforce in collaboration with the region’s governmental forest management office to document illegal activity and conduct patrols.

The team is also developing comprehensive identification manuals and guidelines for regulators. Many existing manuals focus on identifying whole plants and flowers, but traded items can include the orchid’s thickened stem and fleshy underground storage organs, called tubers. Some orchids are boiled, or dried for several hours or days before being traded.

In some parts of Nepal, communities can earn a good income from harvesting and selling orchids alongside other medicinal plants. For many, medicinal plants are their sole source of income. “Simply telling the locals ‘you are not supposed to do this’ will not stop them from harvesting,” Bashyal says. For this reason, imposing a blanket ban on trade might not be effective.

Bashyal emphasizes that tracking the wildlife trade is complex and often requires navigating delicate legal territory. Researchers must also have patience when interviewing informants. “Thus, it also comes down to following research ethics, respect and treating local knowledge as a valuable resource to build trust,” Bashyal says. “Only after that, can we have data and develop any intervention.”

The forests of Makawanpur support an array of native orchids.

The forests of Makawanpur support an array of native orchids.

#774. Bournemouth make European history after coming from behind to beat Celta Vigo

Celta Vigo vs Bournemouth. UEFA Europa League Round 1.

Estadio Abanca-BalaídosAttendance: Attendance20,002.

Report from the Europa League game between Celta Vigo and Bournemouth at Estadio Abanca-Balaidos; Iago Aspas put home side in front before Alvaro Rodriguez and Rayan struck to earn the Cherries a historic victory as Bournemouth extended their winning run to 10 matches in all competitions

Bournemouth continued their magnificent run of form with a 2-1 victory against Celta Vigo, creating two bits of history in the process.

It was a club-record-extending 10th successive win for Bournemouth in all competitions, with the victory also marking the first time an English club have won their first five matches in major European competition.

Veteran former Liverpool striker Iago Aspas put the home side in front in style in the first half, before Bournemouth were reduced to 10 men when Bafode Diakite was sent off for a late challenge.

But Alvaro Rodriguez equalised early in the second half, with substitute Rayan coming on to score a late winner to give Bournemouth an unlikely win.

Bournemouth were fortunate not to go behind after 10 minutes, with an offside flag chalking off Pablo Duran's poke home from close-range.

But the Cherries fell behind 10 minutes later when record Celta Vigo goalscorer Aspas scored a screamer.

The 39-year-old had seen an overhead kick saved well by Michele Di Gregorio, but he picked up the ball on the right side of the area in the second phase of play, before cutting inside to curl past the goalkeeper and into the far corner off the post.

Things went from bad to worse for Bournemouth moment later when Diakite saw a yellow card upgraded to a red after a VAR check following a late challenge on Couhaib Driouech.

Tyler Adams replaced Justin Kluivert at half-time and the tactical switch drew an instant reward when Alvaro Rodriguez glanced home Amine Adli's cross to get Bournemouth back on level terms.

James Hill then drew a fine save from Ionut Radu - who is the only player ever to play for both clubs - before Di Gregorio was called into action at the other end to divert a long-range Aspas strike away.

But three Bournemouth substitutes combined for a late winner.

Adrien Truffert stole possession and broke before finding Marcus Tavernier the area. He laid the ball off for Rayan to sweep home and seal victory as Marco Rose's side made more history with a brilliant win at the Estadio Abanca-Balaidos.

11: GOAL RULED OUT! Duran follows up on an initial shot from Driouech to bundle home but is ruled off-side.

19: GOAL! Veteran striker and former Liverpool man Aspas scores a screamer to give Celta Vigo the lead!

25: RED CARD! Diakite is sent off after a VAR check for a late challenge on Driouech!

30: GOAL RULED OUT! Celta have the ball in the back of the net again, but Duran is again denied by an off-side flag.

39: SAVE! Kluivert shoots from a very tight angle - but it is well saved by Radu in the Celta Vigo goal.

46: GOAL! Rodriguez scores with a glancing header from close-range after a beautiful cross from the right-hand side by Adli.

60: SAVE! Scott goes for goal from a free kick from a tight angle but Radu has it covered.

63: SAVE! Hill has a go from range but the goalkeeper tips over.

73: SAVE! Aspas shoots from the edge of the area and Di Gregorio gets down well to save.

78: GOAL! What a turnaround! Rayan sweeps home to give Bournemouth the lead!

"Now we're enjoying a good run of form and things are going well for us," said Bournemouth midfielder Amine Adli. "We're in a good moment with confidence and a positive atmosphere.

"We're trying to maintain this energy and all the good things we're doing on the pitch, and keep reproducing them in every game."

#773. WWE’s Terri Runnels & Dustin Rhodes Share Death of 3-Year-Old Grandson

WWE wrestler Dustin Rhodes and his ex-wife Terri Runnels shared that their 3-year-old grandson had died: "Please keep us all in your prayers during this time."

Terri Runnels and Dustin Rhodes are facing a devastating loss.

The former WWE wrestling duo shared that their 3-year-old grandson Rowan has died, although they did not share how the toddler passed.

Terri confirmed the news on Facebook, sharing a statement for her and Dustin’s daughter Dakota Runnels and her husband Bleau.

Dustin also asked for prayers for his daughter and her husband, writing in a follow-up message on X, “Guys my grandson Rowan has passed. Please keep us all in your prayers during this time. I am here with @DakotaRunnels22 now.”

The 57-year-old went on to remember the young boy by sharing a photo of himself and Rowan, writing, "Rest in Peace baby boy. I love u so much Rowan."

Terri and Dustin were married from 1993 to 1999. Dustin—the son of WWE Hall of Fame Dusty Rhodes—wrestled for the WWE on and off from 1995 to 2019 under the ring name Goldust. Terri—who was her ex-husband’s manager at the time—joined the WWE under the name Marlena, playing the part of Goldust's cigar-smoking manager.

During her years with the WWE, Terri made sure that she was still able to be there for her daughter, explaining that she told founder Vince McMahon she would not do non-televised shows.

“I wanted to be at home for Dakota,” the 60-year-old told Slam Wrestling in 2021. “Back in the day, Dakota was the only [wrestler’s child] who had both of her parents wrestling. Every other male wrestler had a wife at home that was taking care of the kids, or whatever.”

“Before she was school age, she would fly with me to TVs and pay-per-views,” Terri continued. “Once she got old enough to go to school, I got a live-in nanny. I was comfortable with her being home for three days with the nanny, but then I would be home for four days and I would take over as full-time mom.”

Spurs are getting things moving in the right direction under Roberto De Zerbi - but there's a missing piece to the puzzle

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur’s resurgence under Roberto De Zerbi has breathed fresh life into the club after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

There is one clear deficiency in their current make-up that threatens to limit what they can achieve in 2026/27, though - they can't finish.

Despite sitting comfortably in the top half after 12 games, Spurs’ underlying attacking numbers tell the story of a side creating plenty and squandering too much of it.

Tottenham have rattled off 170 shots in the Premier League this season - the fifth-highest tally in the division - while only Liverpool and Manchester City have registered more efforts from inside the penalty area than Spurs’ 109.

But, when it comes to actually hitting the target, De Zerbi’s side slump to 14th across the top flight.

There's also an issue with their ball-striking. According to Gradient Sports’ analysts, just six of Spurs’ 170 league attempts have been graded as ‘unsaveable’ - a figure bettered by every team in the Premier League bar Everton (5).

For context, high-flying Brighton have racked up 20 unsaveable efforts, while Erling Haaland has managed seven on his own. At 3.5 per cent, Tottenham boast the lowest proportion of unsaveable shots in the entire division.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

A glance at De Zerbi’s attacking options explains why to some extent. Richarlison has been frozen out entirely and is angling for a January move, Dominic Solanke has managed just two league goals, and big-money summer arrival Omar Marmoush is yet to hit the ground running in north London.

Centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is the team's joint-top Premier League goalscorer with two goals after 12 matches: Spurs need a centre-forward in January.

Enter Real Sociedad’s 22-year-old Icelandic international Orri Oskarsson.

Oskarsson is by no means LaLiga’s most prolific frontman, having netted four times in the Spanish top flight this term but his underlying metrics point towards a striker ready to thrive in a possession-heavy, attack-minded system.

Unlike De Zerbi’s Spurs, Real Sociedad do not dominate the ball as often, leaving their striker without service for large periods of matches. Oskarsson, though, is making every second count when his team are in possession, averaging a goal every 64 minutes that La Real actually have the ball this season.

In total, he has scored nine times across his last 13 appearances for club and country.

What makes Oskarsson particularly suited to Tottenham is how intelligently he moves to receive the ball. Gradient Sports’ data shows the Icelandic forward receives line-breaking passes 45 per cent of the time, placing him among LaLiga’s best at peeling off defenders and making himself available to creative midfielders.

That off-the-ball awareness is reinforced by the fact he has received the ball in a clear shooting position 10 times in the league this season - a tally bettered only by Barcelona’s Raphinha (13) and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (11).

Once the ball arrives at his feet, Oskarsson has the penalty-box nous Tottenham lack. Ninety-two per cent of his LaLiga shots this season have been taken from inside the box, which aligns nicely with the 109 close-range openings Spurs have already generated this term. Even more impressive, out of the 25 shots he has taken in LaLiga, five have been graded as unsaveable by Gradient's analysts - just one fewer than Tottenham’s entire squad combined.

Gradient have also flagged just one occasion all season where Oskarsson opted to shoot when passing to a better-placed teammate was the superior option, highlighting good judgement under pressure and decision-making that is rare for a 22-year-old.

Meanwhile, his Expected Goals (xG) ranks sixth-highest in LaLiga - a decent return given Real Sociedad’s modest share of possession and chance creation.

And best of all, a winter deal is entirely plausible. For a Tottenham side creating plenty of penalty-box opportunities but with nobody reliable to tuck them away, Oskarsson could be one of the more shrewd January investments the market has to offer.

Panini have launched their latest Barclays Women's Super League sticker collection, featuring teams from WSL and WSL 2 for a second year running.

This is only the fourth edition of the book for the top women’s league in this country, and Rachel Daly believes the culture of sticker collecting can play its part in growing the women’s game.

As the latest collection was launched in London this week, the ex-Lioness spoke to FourFourTwo about the rise of the women's game.

Speaking at the launch, Daly reflected on her own childhood memories of collecting Panini stickers.

"For me, it goes back to my childhood,” Daly told FourFourTwo. “I collected them with my brother. We used to, every Saturday morning, go and get the stickers.

"You'd get your piles and you'd trade them and swap them at school. Just that whole feeling of sitting down and putting stickers in.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I'm a Leeds fan, so I always wanted to get the whole Leeds team immediately when I was younger.

"I would literally swap any of my stickers, even if I'd already got the Leeds player, just to have more.”

While Daly grew up collecting men’s players, this WSL collection offers an opportunity to introduce more fans to the women's game, something Daly believes is particularly important as the league continues to grow.

The latest album has 545 stickers across all 26 WSL and WSL2 clubs, giving fans access to collect stickers of their favourite players from across the top two tiers of English women’s football.

"The visibility of the game is massive," she added.

"For the fact that it's WSL 1 and 2, I think it's equally as important. Those players in the WSL 2 deserve the same recognition as us.

"Being able to see kids being exposed to seeing the women's game as well, it's exciting."

Daly was speaking at the launch of the Panini Barclays Women's Super League Official Sticker Collection 2027 in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.

#770. US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035

FIFA has confirmed the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will host the 2031 Women's World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams. The UK will stage the 2035 edition, its first World Cup since 1966.

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

The next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

Ten-man Huddersfield moved level at the top of League One with a 3-2 win at Doncaster.

Goals from Cameron Humphreys, Joe Taylor and Ilias Bronkhorst delivered the win despite Town seeing Bali Mumba dismissed before half-time for two bookable offences. The second came when conceding a penalty from which Isaac Hutchinson netted to give Doncaster hope.

Rovers controlled possession from then on but struggled to fashion opportunities and were punished on 59 minutes when Bronkhorst lashed in from a corner, moments after Derensili Sanches Fernandes struck the bar with a fierce effort.

A scruffy finish from Owen Bailey on 89 minutes threatened a late Rovers fightback but Town hung on to draw level with leaders Stockport.

The parallels between the Hammers and the Foxes are impossible to ignore as Scott Parker’s team slide down the Championship table

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.

It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer plan and greater purpose.

Sometimes, though, relegation is just the start. If it is not taken seriously, relegation might not be rock-bottom, but a trapdoor that sends a club spiralling to new lows.

Leicester City know all about that trapdoor. The Foxes were Premier League champions in 2016, FA Cup winners in 2021 and Conference League semi-finalists in 2021/22, but are now in League One after a series of relegations.

They were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware, but years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy saw them fall into the second tier and beyond.

West Ham United were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware - the Conference League in 2023 - but dropped out of the Premier League last season after years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Hammers had been in the division since 2012 and finished as high as sixth in 2020/21, ending the campaign a place and a point behind Leicester. In 2024/25, the season before they went down, they generated the 20th-highest revenue in world football, according to the Deloitte Money League. Leicester were 17th in the Money League in 2021/22, the campaign before the first of their two recent relegations from the Premier League.

Both clubs boast facilities that are out of place in their division. West Ham’s 62,500-seater London Stadium has almost double the capacity of the next biggest Championship ground, while Leicester’s training complex is one of the best in the country, let alone League One.

The parallels do not end there. Like Leicester 12 months ago, West Ham were one of the pre-season Championship promotion favourites and started the campaign well, but those results papered over the cracks.

Since climbing to second with a 1-0 victory at then-leaders Swansea City on October 17, the Hammers have gone six games without a win and sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo, replacing him with Scott Parker. They are 13th ahead of today’s visit of second-place Stoke City, with 24 points from 17 matches.

It is eerily similar to Leicester’s start to last season. Looking to make an immediate return to the Premier League, the Foxes were third on October 17. But like West Ham, results started to slide. Like West Ham, they had 24 points after 17 games.

Of course, Leicester’s season ended with relegation, and the Hammers are by no means destined for the drop. Right now, though, the parallels are impossible to ignore.

In terms of individual quality, both clubs began their respective seasons with one of the most talented squads in the league. Leicester had the likes of Abdul Fatawu, Jordan James and Stephy Mavididi, while West Ham can call on Jarrod Bowen, Konstantinos Mavropanos and Manor Solomon, among others.

However, both squads bore the hallmarks of years of poor recruitment. Leicester’s group included several big-money signings that had failed to deliver, including Patson Daka, Oliver Skipp and Jannik Vestergaard, and they did not pay a single transfer fee in the summer 2025 window to try to balance the books.

Meanwhile, West Ham have a top-heavy squad filled with attacking quality but light on defensive cover. The Hammers spent almost £40million this summer - including paying an EFL-record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic - yet failed to address some glaring gaps in the squad.

With all those attackers, West Ham need a manager who wants to dominate games. But Nuno prefers to let the opponents have the ball and attack quickly in transition, which was ill-suited to his squad. The Hammers have now appointed Parker, a Championship promotion specialist having previously taken Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley up.

Once again, it is strikingly similar to Leicester, who sacked Marti Cifuentes in January and turned to Gary Rowett, a Championship survival specialist. However, his pragmatic style did not get the best out of his players and the Foxes continued to slide.

This runs deeper than the managers, though. Any head coach at Leicester would have struggled to reinvigorate a group of players who had either lost belief or did not want to be at the club anymore.

That showed in their reaction to going behind. After November 8 last year, Leicester did not win a single Championship game in which they conceded first. If heads drop when you suffer a setback, it points to a lack of confidence, fight or both, and form will suffer.

This season, West Ham are yet to win in the league after going 1-0 down, drawing five times and suffering five defeats. They have conceded first in every game of their six-match winless run. This is the biggest red flag of the Hammers’ season so far. Having quality players means nothing if they do not have the right mentality, as Leicester found out last term.

It remains very unlikely that West Ham follow the Foxes into League One. But their recent transfer business does not suggest they will recruit smartly in January and if they miss out on promotion, you would expect some of their better players to leave next summer - sparking a transition period and potentially an extended spell outside of the top flight.

Even if Parker turns it around and wins promotion, is he the right man to lead them in the Premier League? The Hammers manager is yet to succeed in a top-flight job and if he is sacked in 12 months time, you would not back the club’s hierarchy to identify the right replacement based on their track record.

That was another feature of Leicester’s decline. The Foxes won promotion at the first attempt in 2023/24 but made poor managerial choices in Steve Cooper and then Ruud van Nistelrooy, and were relegated immediately.

Five years ago, West Ham fans would have dreamed of being the ‘next Leicester City’. Right now, it is the nightmare scenario.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#766. Vrancken proud of Hearts players despite last-gasp defeat to Monaco

Hearts vs Monaco. UEFA Conference League Round 1.

Tynecastle ParkAttendance: Attendance15,164.

Hearts lost 3-2 at home to Monaco in the Conference League; Jordi Altena opened the scoring; Sabah Kerjota pulled the Jambos back level after goals from Folarin Balogun and Edan Diop; Balogun netted again in stoppage-time; the Jambos have one point from their opening four games

Wouter Vrancken expressed pride in his Hearts team after an agonising 3-2 defeat at home to Monaco left their Conference League hopes hanging by a thread.

The Jambos looked on course to pick up their second league-phase point after stunning first-half strikes from Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota either side of goals from visiting pair Folarin Balogun and Edian Diop.

But in the fourth and final minute of added time, injury-hit Hearts were denied what would have been a hugely commendable result when USA forward Balogun found space in the box to slot home and maintain Monaco's perfect record in the competition.

"The biggest thing is, of course, to be really proud of the performance we put on the park today, because it's against a really good side," said Vrancken, keen to reiterate that his team remains without several key players.

"Knowing that we have still nine injuries, I will mention it, and we have a lot of players not on the European list today and to still do this against that team, I'm really proud of what we did."

A point would have significantly boosted Hearts' hopes of reaching the knockout phase, but they can now only finish on a maximum of seven points - the same tally they managed two years ago before being eliminated on goal difference under Neil Critchley.

With their goal difference currently standing at minus five, Hearts will likely need high-scoring victories against Bosnian side Borac and Cypriot outfit Pafos in their final two matches to stand a chance of breaking into the top 24 and extending their European campaign beyond Christmas.

Vrancken, however, does not believe the late goal will make a significant difference to his side's prospects.

"I think the point doesn't make a difference," he said. "One or no points doesn't change anything in the next games. There's also something that really was pleasing for me, that when it was 2-2, we still wanted to go.

"We wanted to go for the win here, and against a side like this, in the situation we're in, so really proud of this also, because three points would make a difference.

"Zero or one point doesn't make a difference towards the next games, so you have to win the next games."Vrancken believes the quality of the goals scored by Altena and Kerjota, both exquisite finishes from range, highlighted the renewed belief coursing through his squad after their 8-0 win over Dundee last weekend.

"They were quality goals," he said. "You see the confidence those guys have, and this is what we wanted after the weekend, of course, that you take some confidence of the dynamics we did there.

"I think the conviction around the box was there, also in both boxes actually. It's an important thing to take with us towards the next games coming, especially in this run of games."

#765. Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between the US and China.

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.
